notes.meaning: Midday turned completely dark for three hours while Jesus hung on the cross. This was not a regular eclipse, because it took place during the full moon of Passover. The deep darkness was a miracle sent by God to show His horror at the world's sin and Christ's inner agony as He bore God's judgment.

Jesus cried out the opening words of Psalm 22 in His everyday language, asking why God had forsaken Him. He was not losing faith, because He still called God 'My God,' but He was feeling the crushing weight of bearing human sin without the comfort of the Father's presence. By quoting this psalm, He also pointed to its final message of victory.

differ.view: Jesus underwent a genuine forsakenness as He bore our actual sin and God's true wrath in our place.
God withdrew His felt favor and comfort as a judge dealing with a substitute, yet without ever breaking the bond between Father and Son.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some Word of Faith teachers argue that Jesus died spiritually, took on Satan's nature in hell, and had to be born again, though critics reject this as denying His finished work on the cross.

notes.meaning: Some people standing by claimed Jesus was calling for the prophet Elijah. They may have misunderstood His words because 'Eli' sounded like Elijah's name, or they twisted His words on purpose to mock Him.

A person soaked a sponge in cheap, sour wine and lifted it on a stick to offer Jesus a drink for His burning thirst. Others told him to wait and see if Elijah would really come down to rescue Him. This shows that even in His final moments, Jesus was surrounded by cruel mockery.

Jesus shouted once more with strength and then gave up His spirit. A loud voice showed that He was not simply dying from bodily weakness. Instead, He willingly handed over His life to His Father when His work of paying for sin was complete.

The thick temple curtain that blocked the entrance to the Most Holy Place was torn from top to bottom by God's power. This showed that Christ's sacrifice opened the way for all people to come straight into God's presence without need for the old animal offerings. At the same instant, the ground shook violently and boulders cracked apart.

differ.view: The torn veil shows that Old Testament rituals have completely ended and every believer now belongs to a royal priesthood with direct access to God.
The torn veil highlights the removal of the wall separating Jews and Gentiles, giving everyone the same open road to God's mercy seat.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars interpret the torn veil as a sign of judgment marking the departure of God's presence from the temple, or as a symbol that Christ Himself has replaced the temple building.

notes.meaning: The earthquake cracked open burial caves, and many godly believers were raised from the dead. After Jesus Himself rose, they came out of their graves, went into Jerusalem, and showed themselves to many people. This miracle was proof that Christ's death and resurrection had broken the grip of the grave.

differ.view: These believers were likely given new life when the tombs opened at Jesus' death, but stayed back until after His resurrection before entering the city.
The phrase 'after his resurrection' applies only to their walk and appearance in the city, keeping Christ as the firstfruits of the dead.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern critics view the story of the raised saints as a symbolic legend rather than a historical event, while others suggest the earthquake merely exposed buried bones.

notes.meaning: The Roman officer and the soldiers guarding the cross were filled with terror when they felt the earthquake and saw the other wonders. They realized that God was testifying to Jesus, and they confessed that He truly was the Son of God.

A group of women who had traveled with Jesus from Galilee to help take care of Him stood watching the cross from a distance. While the male disciples had scattered in fear, these women stayed faithful to the very end. Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the mother of James and John.

As evening came, a wealthy member of the Jewish council named Joseph of Arimathea stepped forward as a disciple of Jesus. He boldly went to the governor Pilate and asked for the Lord's body so it would not be thrown into an unmarked criminal's pit. Pilate agreed and ordered the body released to him.

Joseph lovingly wrapped the body of Jesus in clean linen cloth and laid it inside his own unused rock-cut tomb. He then rolled a huge stone over the doorway and left. This fulfilled the ancient prophecy of Isaiah 53:9 that the Messiah would be with the rich in His death.
Mary Magdalene and the other Mary stayed behind and sat across from the tomb in deep grief. They carefully marked where Jesus was buried so they could return later with spices after the Sabbath rest.

The next day, during the Sabbath, the chief priests and Pharisees went together to Pilate. They remembered that Jesus had promised to rise after three days, and they warned Pilate that His disciples might steal the body and claim He was alive. They wanted a Roman guard placed around the grave until the third day had passed.

Pilate told the religious leaders to take a squad of guards and make the tomb as secure as they knew how. They stamped the official seal across the stone so no one could touch it, and they set the soldiers to stand watch. In the end, their extreme care only provided solid, undeniable proof that Jesus really rose from the dead.
